title: Starting early and asset classes
blurb: The cost of waiting, the four kinds of assets and a mix that fits a timeline.

levels.title: The cost of waiting
learn: Compare two savers who start at different ages.
Say why the early years are worth the most.

cards.text: Alia and Ravi each save $200.00 a month. Alia saves from age 22 to 32, then stops and never adds again. Ravi starts later, at 32, and saves every month until he is 65. Both earn 7% a year in this example. Who has more at 65?
Count what each puts in. Ravi saves for 33 years and Alia for 10. Ravi puts in $55,200 more, over three times as much. But Alia's first deposit has 43 years until 65, and Ravi's has 33.

Interest is added every month, at 7% divided by 12. Each deposit goes in at the end of a month. Every figure is worked out month by month and shown to the nearest dollar. Alia ends $37,600 ahead, the two balances subtracted.

Alia stopped at 32 with $34,617. She added nothing after that, and her balance still climbed to $346,413 by 65, about 10 times as much. Her early deposits had the most years to grow, and the line gets steeper as the interest earns interest.

Now let one saver put in $200.00 every month until 65 and change only the start age. A later start means fewer deposits and less time for each one. The rate matters too: at 5% in this example Ravi finishes ahead, $201,080 to Alia's $161,157.

Look at what each five more years of waiting costs. Starting at 27 instead of 22 costs $203,127. Starting at 32 instead of 27 costs $143,286. Each step costs less than the one before, because the first years had the most time left. The total keeps adding up.

figure.title: Cost of five more years of waiting

levels.title: Four kinds of assets
learn: Name the four asset classes and what each one does.
Say what you get and what you risk with each.

cards.text: Many things can hold your money. They behave in a few ways, so they are sorted into four groups called asset classes. An asset is something you own that has value. The class decides what the asset pays you and what can go wrong.

Cash and equivalents are money you can reach quickly, like a savings account. A GIC, a loan to a bank for a set term, sits here too: locked until the term ends, it may pay a bit more for that. The danger is slow: at 3% inflation (an example), a $200.00 basket costs $206.00 next year, while your $200.00 stays $200.00.

Fixed income is lending to a government or a company, which then owes you. A bond is such a loan. It pays a set amount on set dates. Lend $1,000.00 at 5% and a year's payment is $50.00. You lose if the borrower fails to pay, or if prices rise faster than the payment. If a company fails, lenders are paid before owners.

Equities are shares: you own part of a business. Owners are paid last, from what remains. A shop takes in $8,000, pays $5,000 in costs and $500 to its lender, leaving $2,500 for the owners. Sometimes nothing remains. One company is one bet. An index fund holds many companies and spreads it.

Real assets and alternatives hold value in a thing: property and gold, and crypto, which fits nowhere else. The test: does the thing pay you? A shop earns a profit, a bond pays interest, a rented house pays rent. A bar of gold or a crypto coin pays nothing, so its value rests on what the next buyer will pay.

Side by side, each class has its own job. Cash is there for money you need soon. Fixed income pays a set amount. Equities share in what a business earns. Real assets hold value in a thing. The next level combines them into a mix.

levels.title: A mix for a timeline
learn: Split 100 points across the four classes.
Say why the time before you need the money shapes the mix.

cards.text: A mix is how you split money across the four classes. Use 100 points, and each point is 1% of the money. A mix of 20 points in cash, 30 in fixed income, 45 in equities and 5 in real assets and alternatives adds to 100 and puts 45% in equities.

Three made-up people each need money at a different time. Sami needs hers in 10 months. Hana needs hers in 8 years. Lars needs his in 41 years. How long until you need the money is your timeline. It is the first question for a mix.

Why does the timeline matter? Equities can fall, and a fall takes time to repair. In the game's Exchange a teacher can stage a market crash that takes 25% off equity funds and 5% off bond funds. Cash stays the same in dollars. Money needed in 10 months cannot wait out a crash.

This gives a rule. The sooner you need the money, the more weight goes to cash and fixed income. The longer you can wait, the more weight equities can carry. Age is not the rule: Sami is 16 but her timeline is shorter than that of a 63-year-old who retires in 2 years.

Mixes for one timeline can differ and still be reasonable. A person 2 years from retiring may keep some equities or go nearly all cash. The rule gives the direction, not one answer. A second question is personal: how big a drop can you sit through? That is risk tolerance.

The game's Exchange has a fund of every company in town, a bond fund and a balanced fund. The balanced fund holds 60 parts equity fund and 40 parts bond fund, one made-up kind of mix. Look at what each fund holds. Nothing here says what to buy.

questions.label: What drives it
questions.prompt: By the rule in this level, what matters most when you choose a mix?

terms.meaning: How long until you need the money back. Also called the time horizon.

questions.hint: Read the rule on the fourth card.

options.text: How old the person is
options.why: Age does not decide it. A 16-year-old can have a shorter timeline than a 63-year-old.

options.text: How soon the money is needed
options.why: Yes. The timeline shapes the mix more than anything else about the person.

options.text: How many classes there are
options.why: There are always four. The question is how to weigh them.

questions.label: Shorter timeline
questions.prompt: Sami is 16 and needs money in 10 months. Another person is 63 and retires in 2 years. Whose timeline is shorter?

terms.meaning: How long until you need the money back. Also called the time horizon.

questions.hint: Put both times in months.

options.text: The 63-year-old's, because she is older
options.why: Age does not set the timeline. Two years is 24 months, more than 10.

options.text: They are the same length
options.why: 10 months and 24 months are not the same.

options.text: Sami's, at 10 months
options.why: Yes. 10 months is shorter than 2 years, which is 24 months.

questions.label: Points in equities
questions.prompt: A mix has 25 points in cash, 35 in fixed income and 5 in real assets and alternatives. The mix adds to 100. What percent is in equities?
questions.hint: The four classes add to 100 points. Subtract the three you know.
questions.why: A mix adds to 100 points, and each point is 1%.
questions.miss: Add the three known classes, then take that from 100.

traps.why: That is the other three classes added. Equities are what remains of the 100.

questions.label: Cash and bonds
questions.prompt: Hana's mix is 20 points cash, 35 fixed income, 40 equities and 5 real assets and alternatives. What percent is in cash and fixed income together?
questions.hint: Add only the two classes the question names.
questions.why: Each point is 1%, so add the two classes' points.
questions.miss: Add the points for cash and fixed income only.

traps.why: That is the equities share. The question asks for cash plus fixed income.

questions.label: Mix for Lars
questions.prompt: Lars needs the money in 41 years, the longest of the three timelines. Which mix follows the rule for him?
questions.hint: Find Lars on the second card, then read the rule on the fourth card.

options.text: 60 cash, 30 fixed income, 10 equities, 0 real assets and alternatives
options.why: That weighs cash most, which suits a short timeline, not the longest.

options.text: 40 cash, 40 fixed income, 20 equities, 0 real assets and alternatives
options.why: That still weighs cash and fixed income most. The longest timeline can carry more equities.

options.text: 10 cash, 20 fixed income, 65 equities, 5 real assets and alternatives
options.why: Yes. Equities carry the most weight, which the longest timeline can allow.

questions.label: Mix for Sami
questions.prompt: Sami needs the money in 10 months, the shortest of the three timelines. Which mix follows the rule for her?
questions.hint: Find Sami on the second card, then read the rule on the fourth card.

options.text: 15 cash, 25 fixed income, 55 equities, 5 real assets and alternatives
options.why: Equities carry most of the weight, which suits a long timeline.

options.text: 70 cash, 25 fixed income, 5 equities, 0 real assets and alternatives
options.why: Yes. Cash and fixed income carry almost all of the weight, as a short timeline calls for.

options.text: 30 cash, 20 fixed income, 40 equities, 10 real assets and alternatives
options.why: Equities and alternatives carry half the weight. A short timeline cannot wait out a fall.

questions.label: After a crash
questions.prompt: A person holds $4,000.00 in an equity fund and $6,000.00 in a bond fund. A crash takes 25% off equity funds and 5% off bond funds. What are the two funds worth together afterwards?
questions.hint: Work out each fund after the crash, then add them.
questions.why: Each fund falls by its own percent, and the two results add.
questions.miss: Apply the 25% fall to one fund and the 5% fall to the other.

traps.why: That takes 25% off the whole $10,000.00. The bond fund fell only 5%.

questions.label: Biggest fall
questions.prompt: Tap the class that fell the furthest from $1,000.00.
questions.hint: Each bar is what the $1,000.00 is worth after the crash.
questions.why: Equities are down to $750.00, a fall of $250.00. Fixed income lost $50.00 and cash lost nothing.
questions.miss: Compare each bar with the $1,000.00 you started with.

questions.label: Same timeline
questions.prompt: Two people both need money in 20 years. One would panic at a big drop and the other would not. What differs between them?

terms.meaning: How big a drop a person can sit through without panicking. It differs from person to person.

questions.hint: Reread the card on risk tolerance.

options.text: Their timelines
options.why: Both need the money in 20 years, so the timelines are the same.

options.text: Their risk tolerance
options.why: Yes. How big a drop a person can sit through is personal, and it differs.

options.text: Their asset classes
options.why: The four classes are the same for everyone.

questions.label: All cash for long
questions.prompt: Lars keeps all of his 41-year money in cash. Which risk from level 2 matters most for him?

terms.meaning: A rise in prices over time, so the same dollars buy less.

questions.hint: Look at the risk listed for cash in level 2.

options.text: Inflation cutting what the money buys
options.why: Yes. Inflation keeps cutting what the dollars buy, and 41 years gives it a lot of time.

options.text: The company failing
options.why: Cash is not a company. That risk belongs to equities and bonds.

options.text: The money being paid out too early
options.why: Cash can be reached at any time. That is not the risk.
